blocks.text: Heart drugs act on different problems: pump failure, ischemic symptoms, abnormal electrical activity, and thrombotic risk. Link each class to its target, physiological effect, clinical purpose, and major harm. Symptom relief and improved long-term outcomes are different claims.

items: Separate heart-failure therapy from relief of congestion
Distinguish rate control, rhythm control, and anticoagulation
Recognize major interactions and monitoring requirements

blocks.title: Scope
blocks.text: An educational overview of adult cardiovascular pharmacology, not a prescribing protocol. No dose or patient-specific regimen is supplied. Guideline statements are identified by their publication year; consult full current guidelines and product labels for clinical use.

blocks.title: Four questions for every drug
rows: Rate, conduction, contraction, vascular tone, fluid, or coagulation
Symptoms, hospitalization, survival, or embolic-risk reduction
Excess target effect, off-target toxicity, interactions, or accumulation

blocks.title: Heart failure: foundational therapy versus congestion

blocks.text: The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA framework for HFrEF includes four foundational classes: renin–angiotensin system inhibition, an evidence-based beta blocker, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and an SGLT2 inhibitor. Diuretics address congestion. This framework does not mean that every drug or dose in these classes is interchangeable.

blocks.title: The HFrEF framework
rows: Renal transporter target; benefits extend beyond glucose lowering

blocks.title: Sacubitril–valsartan: two coordinated targets
blocks.description: Select each arm to compare enzyme inhibition with receptor blockade. [P5]

steps.title: Sacubitril–valsartan
steps.description: One combination with complementary actions.

steps.title: LBQ657
steps.description: Sacubitril is converted to this active metabolite.

steps.title: Neprilysin
steps.description: Inhibition reduces breakdown of substrates including natriuretic peptides.

steps.title: Peptide effects
steps.description: Increased peptide availability supports cardiovascular and renal effects.

steps.title: AT₁ receptor
steps.description: Valsartan blocks angiotensin II signaling at AT₁.

steps.title: Reduced Ang II effects
steps.description: Angiotensin II-dependent effects, including aldosterone release, are attenuated.

blocks.label: ACE inhibitor / ARNI interaction
blocks.text: Sacubitril–valsartan must not overlap with an ACE inhibitor. The label specifies at least 36 hours between switching from or to an ACE inhibitor because of angioedema risk.

blocks.title: Monitoring follows the mechanism
rows: Volume status, renal context, relevant symptoms
Weight / congestion, blood pressure, electrolytes, renal function

blocks.title: Do not use glucose alone to rule out ketoacidosis
blocks.text: SGLT2-associated ketoacidosis can occur without marked hyperglycemia. The drug class has heart-failure benefits independent of diabetes status, but that does not remove its adverse-effect profile.

blocks.prompt: Which item primarily relieves congestion rather than representing one of the four foundational HFrEF classes?
blocks.answer: Loop diuretics treat congestion. Their role is distinct from the foundational HFrEF framework described in the 2022 guideline.

blocks.title: Metoprolol: exposure, beta blockade, and clearance
blocks.description: A qualitative drug journey; node spacing does not represent time or concentration. [P4]

steps.title: Oral formulation
steps.description: This example uses extended-release metoprolol succinate.

steps.title: Systemic exposure
steps.description: Absorption and release characteristics determine exposure over time.

steps.title: β₁ receptor
steps.description: Preferential β₁ blockade reduces catecholamine effects. Selectivity is not absolute.

steps.title: Nodal / cardiac effects
steps.description: Sinus rate and AV conduction slow; cardiac workload is reduced.

steps.title: Hepatic metabolism
steps.description: CYP2D6 activity and inhibitors can change exposure.

steps.title: Elimination
steps.description: Drug-related material leaves the body after metabolism; clearance affects exposure.

blocks.title: Selective does not mean exclusive
blocks.text: At higher concentrations, metoprolol also blocks β₂ receptors. Bradycardia, conduction disturbance, hypotension, and bronchospasm risk remain relevant. Abrupt withdrawal can aggravate ischemia.

blocks.label: Formulation matters
blocks.text: Metoprolol succinate extended release is the metoprolol formulation in the evidence-based HFrEF framework. Do not silently substitute a different formulation or assume all beta blockers have equivalent outcome evidence.

blocks.title: Angina: reduce demand, modify vascular tone

blocks.text: The 2023 chronic-coronary-disease guideline identifies a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker as first-line antianginal therapy. Long-term beta-blocker use does not automatically improve outcomes in every patient with chronic coronary disease; the indication depends on factors such as recent MI, ventricular function, and other primary indications.

blocks.title: Nitroglycerin: from sublingual entry to lower preload
blocks.description: Grouped pharmacodynamic sequence, not a dosing or emergency-treatment algorithm. [P9]

steps.title: Sublingual entry
steps.description: Absorption through oral mucosa.

steps.title: NO signaling
steps.description: Bioactivation produces NO signaling.

steps.title: Guanylate cyclase
steps.description: NO increases smooth-muscle cGMP.

steps.title: Vascular relaxation
steps.description: Smooth muscle relaxes.

steps.title: Venous pooling
steps.description: Predominant venous dilation lowers venous return.

steps.title: Lower preload
steps.description: LV filling pressure falls.

blocks.title: Calcium channel blockers are not one physiological group
rows: Vascular smooth-muscle relaxation; edema is a characteristic adverse effect
More prominent nodal / cardiac effects; bradycardia and AV block are concerns

blocks.label: High-risk nitrate combination
blocks.text: Nitrates are contraindicated with PDE-5 inhibitors and soluble guanylate-cyclase stimulators such as riociguat because of severe hypotension risk.

blocks.title: Two nodal brakes can add
blocks.text: Diltiazem or verapamil with a beta blocker can produce excessive slowing of conduction or heart rate. Negative inotropic effects also matter when ventricular function is impaired. Non-dihydropyridine CCBs are generally avoided in HFrEF because of negative inotropy.

blocks.title: The classic antiarrhythmic class map
rows: Flecainide (IC): slows conduction; structural-heart-disease context matters
Diltiazem / verapamil: prominent AV nodal effects

blocks.title: Antiarrhythmics can cause arrhythmias
blocks.text: Flecainide has important proarrhythmic risk, particularly in relevant structural-heart-disease or prior-MI settings. Sotalol can prolong QT and cause torsades de pointes; renal function, potassium, magnesium, and ECG monitoring matter. Class labels do not establish interchangeability.

blocks.title: Mechanism-focused examples
rows: AV nodal slowing; not suitable for every ventricular-function context
Can interrupt AV-node-dependent reentry; not a general AF conversion drug
Pulmonary, hepatic, thyroid, and cardiac toxicity
Inotropy plus AV nodal slowing; narrow safety margin

blocks.title: Digoxin: inotropy and nodal effects are distinct
blocks.description: A simplified mechanism map. Increased contraction and slowed AV conduction arise through different causal chains. [P12, P18]

steps.title: Digoxin
steps.description: A cardiac glycoside with a narrow therapeutic margin.

steps.title: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase
steps.description: Digoxin inhibits the membrane sodium pump.

steps.title: Intracellular Ca²⁺
steps.description: Altered Na⁺ handling reduces Ca²⁺ extrusion through Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange.

steps.title: Increased inotropy
steps.description: More available calcium increases contraction force.

steps.title: Autonomic effects
steps.description: Parasympathetic effects contribute to nodal slowing.

steps.title: Slower AV conduction
steps.description: Nodal effects are distinct from increased myocardial contraction.

blocks.title: Digoxin toxicity is contextual
blocks.text: Renal impairment can increase digoxin exposure. Electrolyte abnormalities, particularly hypokalemia, increase susceptibility to toxicity. Nausea, visual disturbance, bradyarrhythmias, or other arrhythmias can be clues.

blocks.title: Amiodarone is a multi-organ drug
blocks.text: Although often grouped as class III, amiodarone has multiple electrophysiological actions. Pulmonary toxicity, liver injury, thyroid dysfunction, bradycardia, and interactions require attention. Its effects and interactions can persist after discontinuation.

blocks.prompt: Why can digoxin increase contraction force while slowing AV nodal conduction?
options: Its ionic and autonomic effects involve different causal pathways
blocks.answer: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition increases calcium availability in myocardium, while indirect autonomic effects contribute to nodal slowing.

blocks.prompt: What is adenosine most directly suited to interrupt in this mechanism overview?
blocks.answer: Transient AV nodal suppression can terminate appropriate AV-node-dependent supraventricular reentry. Rhythm identification and contraindications remain essential.

blocks.title: Thrombosis and prevention: a separate axis

blocks.text: In atrial fibrillation, ventricular rate control, rhythm control, and embolic-risk reduction are separate decisions. The 2023 AF guideline generally favors DOACs over warfarin when anticoagulation is indicated, except in mechanical-valve recipients or patients with moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis.

blocks.title: Do not interchange therapeutic categories
rows: P2Y12 inhibition reduces platelet activation; bleeding risk remains
DOAC or warfarin, according to indication
HMG-CoA reductase inhibition lowers LDL-related risk
Treat electrical behavior; does not replace indicated anticoagulation

blocks.label: A controlled pulse does not settle stroke risk
blocks.text: Successful rate control or restoration of sinus rhythm does not by itself determine whether anticoagulation is indicated. Assess thromboembolic risk and clinical context separately.

blocks.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes an antiarrhythmic from an anticoagulant?
options: Both primarily block platelet P2Y12 receptors
Rhythm drugs address electrical behavior; anticoagulants address thromboembolic risk
All rhythm drugs prevent embolic stroke
blocks.answer: Electrical control and embolic prevention are different treatment goals. One does not automatically substitute for the other.

blocks.title: Four recurring failure modes
rows: RAAS inhibitor + MRA in a vulnerable setting
Reduced potassium excretion; monitoring is essential
Digoxin with renal impairment / low potassium
Clearance and electrolyte context change toxicity risk

blocks.prompt: What minimum ACE-inhibitor separation is specified in the sacubitril–valsartan label?
blocks.answer: At least 36 hours when switching from or to an ACE inhibitor. Avoid concomitant use because of angioedema risk.

blocks.title: Can you explain the clinical logic?
items: I can identify the four foundational HFrEF classes
I can distinguish congestion relief from outcome evidence
I can trace a nitrate, beta blocker, and digoxin mechanism
I can explain why rate control does not replace anticoagulation
I can name the major dangerous combinations
I can connect renal function and electrolytes to drug toxicity

blocks.title: How to use this lecture
blocks.text: Examples are selective rather than an exhaustive cardiovascular formulary. The step processes group mechanisms and omit quantitative PK/PD, doses, and individualized selection. The source key identifies the guidelines and labels used; clinical decisions require the full relevant documents.
